extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers, and practitioners interested in comedy and humor studies
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive overview of what constitutes off-color (vulgar/crude/shock) humor: its defining topics, typical forms, purpose, historical context, and cultural variants. Useful for identifying, classifying, or producing off-color comedic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of off-color humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Off-color humor (also known as vulgar humor, crude humor, crass humor, coarse humor or shock humor) is humor that deals with topics that may be considered to be in poor taste or vulgar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core definitional criterion: material qualifies as off-color when its subject matter is broadly regarded as vulgar or in poor taste. The page lists common synonyms to indicate overlapping labels and usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common off-color topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Most commonly labeled as 'off-color' are acts concerned with sex, a particular ethnic group, or gender. Other off-color topics include violence, particularly domestic abuse; excessive swearing or profanity; toilet humor; national superiority or inferiority, pedophilic content, and any topics generally considered impolite or indecent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether a joke/bit is off-color, check whether it targets or relies on these subjects. The list signals typical content triggers for offensiveness and social taboo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose: induce shock and surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, the point of off-color humor is to induce laughter by evoking a feeling of shock and surprise in the comedian's audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess off-color material by whether it intentionally aims for shock/surprise as the mechanism for eliciting laughter; this distinguishes it from benign or purely observational humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms and genres that incorporate off-color elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Many comedic genres (including jokes, prose, poems, black comedy, blue comedy, insult comedy, cringe comedy and skits) may incorporate 'off-color' elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Off-color techniques can appear across formats — stand-up, sketches, cartoons, TV shows, films, poems, etc. Evaluation should consider genre conventions and medium-specific constraints (e.g., TV censorship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and cultural variation in acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Dirty jokes were once considered subversive and underground, and rarely heard in public. American society has become increasingly tolerant of off-color humor since that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptability is time- and culture-dependent. When judging or producing off-color content, take historical context and prevailing social norms into account (examples: Lenny Bruce's obscenity trial; mainstreaming in the 1970s–1990s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use as social commentary or critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedians such as George Carlin and Richard Pryor have used [off-color humor] as an effective tool for social commentary. In the 1990s and modern era, comedians have used shocking content to draw attention to their criticism of social issues, especially censorship and the socioeconomic divide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One evaluative dimension is whether offensiveness serves a critical or satirical purpose rather than gratuitous shock. Material that uses taboo subjects to illuminate social issues can be judged differently from material that merely seeks to offend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques/styles within off-color humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Different styles include shocking content, absurdist off-color humor, outrageous stunts and grotesque or gross-out depictions (e.g., Tom Green's stunts; Dave Attell and Louis C.K.'s absurdism; Beavis and Butt-head's animal-cruelty depictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the technique (shock, absurdism, gross-out, stunt-based, extended improvisational 'dirty joke' routines like 'The Aristocrats') to evaluate intent, audience reaction, and risk of backlash or censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and censorship risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Off-color humor has led to legal consequences (e.g., Lenny Bruce was tried, convicted, and jailed for obscenity after a stand-up performance that included off-color humor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating off-color material, consider legal exposure and likely responses from venues, broadcasters, and regulators in the relevant jurisdiction and era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural labeling: 'veg' vs 'non-veg' jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: In some parts of the world, sexual humor in particular is known as 'non-veg' humor, contrasted with the 'veg' jokes that are more acceptable in polite company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cultural label signals a local classificatory system for acceptability; creators/evaluators should be sensitive to regional terminology and norms when judging sexual/off-color jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to taboo and political correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: In British humor, the genre of 'sick jokes' is often used to shock by poking fun at taboo or as a reaction against political correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One criterion is whether off-color material functions as transgression against taboos or as deliberate pushback against political-correctness norms; this affects both audience reception and critical interpretation.
